scenarios.scenario_text: Provider and Recipient are engaged in discussions regarding a Possible Transaction. During these discussions, Provider shares Evaluation Material with Recipient, including sensitive financial data, personnel information, and operational strategies. Recipient ensures that all its Representatives sign written acknowledgments agreeing to be bound by the terms of the agreement. However, during a strategy meeting, a Representative of Recipient creates a detailed presentation summarizing the Evaluation Material, including Provider’s financial projections and personnel assessments. This presentation is shared via a secure internal collaboration platform that allows for real-time editing by multiple team members. While the platform is encrypted and access is restricted to authorized Representatives, the platform’s auto-backup feature stores copies of the presentation on a third-party cloud server. Separately, Provider requests that all Evaluation Material be destroyed or returned. Recipient complies by deleting the original files and shredding physical copies but does not delete the presentation stored on the cloud server, believing it qualifies as a document retained for 'archival, legal, and compliance purposes.' Provider later discovers the existence of the presentation on the cloud server and raises concerns about the potential breach of confidentiality and improper handling of Evaluation Material.

clauses.evidence_3: Without prior written consent of the other Parties, none of the Parties may assign any or all of its rights and obligations under this Agreement to any third party.

scenarios.scenario_text: Party A, a signatory to a multi-party agreement, decided to outsource its customer service obligations to a third-party vendor, Company Z. Aware of the requirement to obtain prior written consent from the other Parties (Party B and Party C), Party A sent a formal notice via email to both Parties, requesting their written consent. Party B promptly responded with explicit written approval. However, Party C did not respond to the email directly. In an effort to expedite the process, Party A's representative, Alex, reached out to Chris, Party C’s representative, via text message. In the exchange, Chris replied, 'I don’t see any issues with this—feel free to proceed.' Party A interpreted this text message as implicit consent, reasoning that the clause did not explicitly define the format of 'written consent.' To ensure transparency, Alex documented the text conversation in an internal memo and forwarded a summary of the text exchange to both Party B and Party C. Neither Party B nor Party C raised objections to the forwarded summary. Believing all obligations under the agreement were satisfied, Party A proceeded with the assignment to Company Z. Several months later, a dispute arose when Party C argued that the assignment was invalid due to the absence of its prior written consent as required under the clause: 'Without prior written consent of the other Parties, none of the Parties may assign any or all of its rights and obligations under this Agreement to any third party.' Party C claimed that its consent via text message did not meet the standard of 'prior written consent' under the agreement’s terms. Party A defended its actions, asserting that the text message was a form of written communication, especially since Party C never objected to the forwarded summary of the exchange.

scenarios.scenario_text: Achaogen and Microgenics entered into an agreement wherein Achaogen agreed to pay Microgenics for any shortfall in Minimum Threshold Revenue during the applicable Minimum Threshold Periods, on a prorated basis, as applicable. In the fiscal year 2023, Microgenics experienced a $1.8 million shortfall in the Minimum Threshold Revenue in the EU region. Achaogen calculated a prorated payment of $1.45 million, factoring in deductions for discounts, allowances, and promotional rebates, which were documented as permissible under GAAP. However, Achaogen also applied an additional deduction for 'anticipated returns' based on forecasted market conditions, arguing that these returns, though not yet materialized, were reasonably foreseeable and should be accounted for to ensure accurate financial reporting. This adjustment reduced the payment to $1.2 million. Achaogen communicated this calculation through a formal payment notice accompanied by a detailed spreadsheet, which included an explanatory note justifying the deductions. The payment was issued within the agreed-upon timeline. Microgenics, upon review, contested the inclusion of 'anticipated returns,' arguing that such adjustments were speculative and not explicitly provided for in the agreement. Achaogen countered this by stating that the deductions were made in good faith and were consistent with their standard accounting practices. Microgenics escalated the matter, claiming the deduction breached the intent of the revenue-sharing provision, as the agreement only allowed for deductions directly tied to actual sales, without explicitly mentioning projected adjustments.

scenarios.scenario_text: Company A and Company B are engaged in discussions regarding a potential acquisition (the 'Possible Transaction'). As part of these discussions, Company A shares Evaluation Materials with Company B under a confidentiality agreement containing the Multi-Conditional Obligation clause. During the negotiation process, a journalist contacts a senior executive at Company B, asking whether Company B is in acquisition talks with Company A. The executive, attempting to maintain confidentiality, responds, 'We are always exploring opportunities in the market, and we are currently in discussions with several companies about potential transactions.' Separately, Company B's legal team submits a mandatory filing to a government agency disclosing that it is evaluating a potential acquisition in the industry, naming Company A as one of the entities involved. The legal team argues that naming Company A was necessary to comply with a specific regulatory requirement that mandates transparency about counterparties in certain types of filings. This filing is publicly accessible and explicitly links Company B to Company A. Later, Company A accuses Company B of breaching the confidentiality agreement, citing both the public filing and the executive's statement to the journalist as evidence of disclosure. Company B defends its actions, claiming that the filing was required by law and the executive's statement was sufficiently vague to avoid revealing specific facts about the Possible Transaction.

scenarios.scenario_text: Party A and Party B entered into a service agreement governed by the clause: 'Upon expiration of the Initial Term, unless written notice to the contrary is provided by one party to the other party at least 30 days prior to the expiration of the then-current term, this Agreement shall be renewed for additional, successive periods of one (1) year each.' The Initial Term was set to expire on March 31, 2024. On February 28, 2024, Party A decided to provide written notice of non-renewal through a physical letter sent via courier. The letter was addressed to Party B’s headquarters and marked as 'Non-Renewal Notice.' The courier company confirmed delivery to the reception desk of Party B’s corporate offices at 3:45 PM on February 28, 2024. However, the letter was mistakenly placed in the wrong department’s internal mail bin and did not reach Party B’s legal team until April 2, 2024. In the interim, Party B acted as though the agreement had automatically renewed, issuing new invoices for services beginning on April 1, 2024. Party A argued that their delivery of written notice through a reputable courier service fulfilled their contractual obligation, as the agreement did not specify a method of delivery beyond 'written notice.' Party B countered that the notice was not properly received by the relevant party within the required timeframe, invalidating the non-renewal and triggering automatic renewal under the terms of the contract.

scenarios.scenario_text: ExxonMobil and FCE entered into a licensing agreement governing the use of Generation 2 Technology for Carbon Capture Applications. Per Clause 7.01(b)(2), ExxonMobil is required to grant FCE a worldwide, non-exclusive, royalty-bearing, non-sub-licensable, non-transferable right and license to practice Program Results for Carbon Capture Applications, but only upon FCE's written request and ExxonMobil's formal decision not to pursue Generation 2 Technology for Carbon Capture Applications. Eight months into the agreement, ExxonMobil sent an email to its internal leadership stating that 'budgetary constraints make immediate continuation of Generation 2 Technology for Carbon Capture Applications infeasible,' but stopped short of explicitly stating that the project was formally abandoned. This email was inadvertently forwarded to FCE during a routine contract discussion. Believing this statement to constitute a formal decision, FCE sent a written request for the license, citing Clause 7.01(b)(2). ExxonMobil internally debated whether the email qualified as a formal decision but ultimately decided to interpret it as sufficient notice for triggering the clause. Consequently, ExxonMobil began negotiations with FCE for the license. However, the negotiations stalled when ExxonMobil insisted on royalty rates significantly above market standards, citing the clause's requirement for 'commercially reasonable terms.' After weeks of impasse, FCE escalated by filing a notice of dispute, arguing that ExxonMobil's initial email was ambiguous and did not meet the threshold of a formal decision as required under the agreement. FCE further alleged that ExxonMobil's excessive royalty demands were in bad faith. While ExxonMobil argued that its interpretation of the clause was reasonable and that it had fulfilled its obligation to negotiate, FCE maintained that the lack of a clear, formal decision rendered the entire process invalid.

scenarios.scenario_text: ENERGOUS and DIALOG are parties to a licensing agreement that allows DIALOG to use ENERGOUS’ intellectual property under specific conditions. During the Term of the agreement, DIALOG discovers a critical Epidemic Defect in its flagship product, which significantly impacts production yield and quality. To address this issue, DIALOG engages a third-party manufacturing subcontractor, SubTech, to develop a fix. Unlike the compliant path of providing direct and explicit written notice to ENERGOUS about engaging SubTech, DIALOG opts for a streamlined approach to avoid delays. It includes SubTech in an internal email chain with ENERGOUS' engineering liaison, outlining the defect resolution plan and discussing technical details of the fix. The email subject line reads: 'Critical Fix Collaboration—SubTech Added for Immediate Defect Resolution,' and the body of the email emphasizes the urgency of the situation. ENERGOUS’ liaison acknowledges the email but does not escalate or formally respond to the inclusion of SubTech. SubTech proceeds to access the Deposit Materials and implements the required fixes. During this period, DIALOG ensures all royalty payments are made promptly and in full, and the defect is successfully resolved, restoring product quality and yield. Months later, ENERGOUS conducts an internal audit and raises concerns about DIALOG’s compliance with the sublicensing terms. Specifically, ENERGOUS alleges that the inclusion of SubTech in the email chain does not constitute valid written notice and that allowing SubTech to access the Deposit Materials without explicit prior written consent exceeds the permissible scope of sublicensing under the agreement. DIALOG argues that involving SubTech in the email chain, with ENERGOUS' liaison copied, constituted sufficient notice under the circumstances and that its actions were in alignment with the agreement’s purpose of resolving Epidemic Defects while maintaining royalty payments.

scenarios.scenario_text: Customer entered into a Facility Addendum with Manufacturer for an initial term of four years, with the option to extend for up to three additional periods of twelve months each. Thirteen months before the expiration of the Initial Term, Customer sent a formal written notice via email to Manufacturer’s designated contract liaison, stating their intent to extend the agreement for another twelve months. The email had the subject line ‘Notice of Extension’ and explicitly stated, ‘Per the terms of the Facility Addendum, we hereby notify you of our intent to extend the agreement for an additional twelve months.’ Manufacturer acknowledged receipt of the email three business days later. However, one week after sending the email, Customer initiated a restructuring of its internal project teams and reassigned its contract management responsibilities to a new department. During the handover process, the Customer’s new contract liaison realized that the original notice had referenced the wrong expiration date for the Initial Term in the body of the email, listing an expiration date that was two months earlier than the actual date specified in the Facility Addendum. Believing the discrepancy was immaterial because the intent to extend was clear, the new liaison did not send a corrected notice. Manufacturer operated under the extended terms for four months before auditing the contract and identifying the date discrepancy. Manufacturer subsequently claimed that the original notice was invalid because it failed to meet the precise Temporal Condition of providing notice ‘not less than twelve (12) months prior to the expiration of the Initial Term.’ Customer argued that the intent to extend had been communicated unambiguously and that Manufacturer’s initial acknowledgment of the email demonstrated acceptance of the notice.

clauses.evidence_3: Notwithstanding the foregoing, UTK may assign this Agreement or any portion of its Compensation as outlined herein to its subsidiaries in its sole discretion.

scenarios.scenario_text: Company A and Company B entered into an agreement where Company A provides specialized consulting services to Company B. The agreement includes the Multi-Conditional Obligation clause, which specifies: 'Notwithstanding the foregoing, UTK may assign this Agreement or any portion of its Compensation as outlined herein to its subsidiaries in its sole discretion.' UTK, a subsidiary of Company A, was responsible for processing compensation payments under the agreement. Midway through the contract, UTK decided to assign payment processing duties to another subsidiary, UTK Payments LLC, as part of an internal cost optimization initiative. However, rather than directly assigning the responsibility to UTK Payments LLC, UTK entered into a subcontracting arrangement where UTK Payments LLC would act as an intermediary but would further delegate the payment processing to an external third-party payment provider, FinFlow Inc. Company B was informed of UTK Payments LLC’s involvement through a formal notification, which included all relevant details and carried the proper signatures. However, the subcontracting of payment processing to FinFlow Inc. was not disclosed to Company B. Payments made by FinFlow Inc. were timely and accurate, and there was no apparent disruption to Company B’s operations. UTK justified the arrangement by arguing that the clause allowed assignment 'to its subsidiaries in its sole discretion,' and since UTK Payments LLC was a subsidiary, the ultimate delegation to FinFlow Inc. was merely an operational detail and not subject to disclosure. Company B’s compliance department flagged the situation upon noticing FinFlow Inc.'s name in payment confirmations and questioned whether the undisclosed involvement of a non-subsidiary third party violated the terms of the agreement. UTK maintained that the clause conferred broad discretion on assignments, including operational delegation under its subsidiary's supervision, and claimed no breach occurred.

scenarios.scenario_text: Green Cross and MacroGenics were actively collaborating on the prosecution and maintenance of Jointly Owned Patents pursuant to their licensing agreement. MacroGenics' outside counsel, approved by Green Cross, was tasked with preparing a critical patent filing related to a breakthrough product. Green Cross provided extensive comments on the draft filing, including a recommendation to include a specific technical claim that would broaden the scope of protection. MacroGenics' outside counsel, after consulting with MacroGenics' internal IP team, decided to omit this claim, arguing that it might complicate ongoing negotiations with a potential licensing partner in Europe. Instead of formally discussing this decision with Green Cross or providing detailed reasoning, MacroGenics noted in the shared document, 'Claim excluded due to strategic considerations; not suitable for current filing.' While Green Cross discovered the omission during the final review before submission, the timeline for filing was tight, and the document was submitted without the additional claim. Green Cross later accused MacroGenics of failing to comply with its obligation to incorporate 'all reasonable comments' per the agreement. MacroGenics defended its actions by asserting that the omitted claim was not 'reasonable' as it posed significant commercial risks and that its discretion under the clause allowed such decisions to be made unilaterally when justified by strategy. Additionally, MacroGenics argued that the shared document notation fulfilled the requirement to keep Green Cross informed, as the agreement did not explicitly mandate formal communication procedures for such decisions.

clauses.evidence_6: E.piphany allows for unlimited calls to its technical support desk by the HSNS personnel designated under Section 5.7 ("HSNS Responsibilities.")

scenarios.scenario_text: E.piphany, a technical support provider, faced an unexpected surge of calls from HSNS personnel designated under Section 5.7 of their agreement. To address the high volume and minimize wait times, E.piphany implemented a new 'priority routing system,' allowing HSNS personnel to flag urgent issues via email and receive priority callbacks. This adjustment was communicated through an email to HSNS personnel, explaining that flagged emails would bypass the standard queue and receive immediate attention. However, E.piphany’s internal system automatically routed flagged emails to its general support inbox rather than its designated technical support desk, where personnel specially trained for HSNS issues worked. The general support team, unfamiliar with the specific requirements of HSNS cases, handled the flagged emails without escalating them to the technical support desk. HSNS personnel continued to use this flagged email system under the belief that their issues were being handled by the designated technical support personnel. HSNS management later discovered discrepancies in the resolution quality of urgent cases and raised concerns that the flagged emails were not directed to the technical support desk as required by the agreement. E.piphany defended its actions by arguing that the flagged email system was merely an operational adjustment designed to expedite urgent cases and did not explicitly violate the clause, as the agreement did not specify that urgent communications must only pass through the designated technical support desk.

clauses.evidence_1: This Agreement shall automatically be renewed for successive one (1) year increments unless either party request in writing, at least ninety (90) days prior to the anniversary date, that this Agreement not to be renewed.
clauses.evidence_2: This Agreement shall automatically be renewed for successive one (1) year increments unless either party request in writing, at least ninety (90) days prior to the anniversary date, that this Agreement not to be renewed.

scenarios.scenario_text: Party A and Party B are engaged in a service agreement governed by two identical clauses stipulating automatic renewal unless written notice is provided at least ninety (90) days before the anniversary date. Party A, intending to terminate the agreement, mails a certified letter to Party B exactly ninety (90) days prior to the anniversary date, as calculated using Party A’s local calendar. However, Party A mistakenly assumes the postmark date fulfills the temporal condition outlined in the agreement, rather than the date Party B physically receives the letter. Due to postal delays, Party B does not receive the letter until eighty-eight (88) days before the anniversary date in their jurisdiction. To complicate matters, the letter’s subject line reads 'Contract Update Request,' and the termination language is buried in the third paragraph, making it easy to misinterpret as a routine inquiry rather than a termination notice. Party B initially files the letter under general correspondence, only reviewing it after the ninety-day deadline has passed. Party A follows up with a phone call five days later to confirm receipt and clarify termination intent, but Party B insists the original notice was invalid and that the agreement should automatically renew. Party A argues that the postmark date satisfies the ninety-day requirement and that the follow-up call reinforces their termination intent.

clauses.evidence_3: Subject to the terms contained herein, PAPA JOHN'S and ABG agree and acknowledge that during the Term of this Agreement and for one (1) year thereafter, ABG shall be prohibited from granting any rights for CELEBRITY identical or similar to the rights granted to PAPA JOHN'S hereunder to any entity other than PAPA JOHN'S for the purpose of directly promoting, advertising, making an appearance on behalf of, or endorsing Competitive Products; provided, however, that in the event this Agreement is terminated pursuant to Section 7.B. of this Agreement, the prohibition referenced above shall be for a period of six (6) months, except that the prohibition shall referenced above shall not apply (or shall immediately cease to apply, as applicable) in the event of any one or more of the following: (i) the Agreement is terminated due to PAPA JOHN'S failure to pay to ABG any monies under this Agreement, as set forth herein, (ii) the Agreement is terminated due to PAPA JOHN'S failure to grant, issue, or cause to vest any of the RSUs (as hereinafter defined) under this Agreement, as set forth herein, (iii) PAPA JOHN'S failure to pay to ABG any monies under Section 7.D.a. or Section 7.D.b. of this Agreement, as set forth herein, or (iv) PAPA JOHN'S failure to grant, issue, or cause to vest any of the RSUs under Section 7.E.a. or Section 7.E.b. of this Agreement, as set forth herein.

scenarios.scenario_text: PAPA JOHN'S and ABG entered into a sponsorship agreement involving a celebrity endorsement. The agreement prohibited ABG from granting similar endorsement rights for Competitive Products to any entity other than PAPA JOHN'S for one year after termination, except if the termination occurred due to specific failures by PAPA JOHN'S, in which case the restriction would shorten to six months or immediately cease to apply. Midway through the agreement, PAPA JOHN'S faced financial setbacks and delayed payment under Sections 7.D.a and 7.D.b. ABG, seeking clarity, sent a formal letter citing non-payment under Section 7.D.b. as grounds for termination and explicitly stated that the six-month restriction would apply instead of the one-year prohibition. However, ABG simultaneously issued a second notice referencing Section 7.E.a., which stated that failure to grant RSUs could also trigger immediate cessation of the prohibition. The second notice contained ambiguous language about the cessation timeline, stating, 'We interpret the prohibition as ceasing effective immediately under Section 7.E.a.' Without waiting to reconcile the two notices, ABG signed a competing endorsement deal with a rival pizza chain three months after the agreement’s termination. PAPA JOHN'S contested this, claiming ABG breached the agreement by granting rights prematurely, as the first notice unambiguously required a six-month restriction. ABG countered that the second notice under Section 7.E.a. superseded the first, and the prohibition ceased immediately. The dispute hinges on whether ABG violated the precedence rules of the multi-conditional clauses by acting on the ambiguous second notice rather than adhering to the explicit terms of the first.

clauses.evidence_5: During the Term of this Agreement, and for a period of two (2) years thereafter, Aucta shall not research, develop, manufacture, file, sell, market, or distribute more than two products containing the active ingredient Lamotrigine; nor will Aucta directly or indirectly assist any other Person or entity in carrying or any such activities.
clauses.evidence_7: In addition, within twenty-five (25) months after the termination or expiration of the Term and on a Product-by-Product basis, ETON shall perform a final "true-up" reconciliation and shall provide Aucta with a written report of such outlining the deductions specified in the definition of Net Sales. | After termination is effective and Aucta assumes control of the Product, ETON will provide, to the extent practicable, transition services to Aucta to include assistance with Product distribution, processing of rebates, drug safety, etc. at Aucta's cost for such services, for a reasonable period of time as mutually determined by the Parties but not to exceed one hundred eighty (180) days following termination so that Aucta can get its own such services in place. | If this Agreement is terminated by Aucta under Section 11.2 or 11.3, then (a) ETON shall have the right to, and Aucta shall hereby grant ETON a license to, Market or otherwise dispose of any existing inventory of any Products then in ETON's possession subject to paying all Royalties and other amounts due hereunder for such sales, (b) Aucta may keep all the payments under Section 6 paid by ETON up to the point of termination and for ETON's disposal of remaining inventory and Aucta is free to commercialize or relicense the Product with no further obligations owed to ETON, (c) ETON shall refrain from holding itself out as Aucta's distributor, in particular, eliminate any reference to the Product and Aucta from its business, trade style and promotional material, and (d) ETON shall transfer all rights, licenses within thirty (30) days of termination.

scenarios.scenario_text: ETON and Aucta entered into a licensing and distribution agreement involving products containing the active ingredient Lamotrigine. Under the agreement, Aucta was prohibited from researching, developing, or marketing more than two Lamotrigine-containing products during the Term and for two years thereafter (evidence_5). Additionally, ETON was obligated to perform a final 'true-up' reconciliation within 25 months of termination and assist Aucta with product transition services for up to 180 days post-termination (evidence_7). The agreement was terminated on January 1, 2023. On December 20, 2024 (23.75 months post-termination), ETON submitted a 'true-up' report via a formal email titled 'Final Reconciliation Report,' attaching a PDF document with detailed deductions and summaries. However, the document contained a clause stating 'Draft Status - Subject to Final Review.' This created ambiguity about whether the report met the finality requirement under evidence_7. Concurrently, Aucta launched a third Lamotrigine product on January 2, 2025, claiming the two-year prohibition expired on December 31, 2024. However, Aucta had already begun pre-launch marketing activities for the product on December 15, 2024, in the form of press releases and physician outreach campaigns. Aucta defended these actions by asserting that pre-launch marketing did not constitute 'marketing' under evidence_5's prohibitions, as the actual sale of the product occurred only after the two-year restriction expired. ETON did not raise objections to the pre-launch marketing but later claimed that Aucta's actions violated the agreement. This scenario introduces ambiguity in the timing and interpretation of obligations under the contract, particularly regarding the overlap of ETON's 'true-up' report submission and Aucta's marketing restrictions.

In the second year following the Launch Date, ACSI, through one of its Affiliates, initiated a campaign to deliver Amazon.com-branded e-mails and in-product advertising materials related to the Spoken-Word Audio Sub-Section. The Affiliate chosen for this campaign was a prominent data analytics firm specializing in customer segmentation. To maximize efficiency and engagement, the Affiliate used its proprietary AI-based predictive model to identify 10,000 high-value customers from Amazon’s global database. However, instead of directly emailing these customers, the Affiliate embedded the promotional content into a larger multi-brand promotional campaign that was sent via email. The emails featured Amazon.com branding but included offers from multiple unrelated companies within the same email body. The Affiliate justified this approach by arguing that bundling promotions from multiple brands significantly improved open rates and customer engagement metrics. 

For the in-product advertising materials, the Affiliate delivered the content through an innovative browser-based notification system that appeared on the user's device when they visited the Affiliate’s web portal. While the materials prominently displayed Amazon.com branding and adhered to the Spoken-Word Audio Sub-Section’s theme, the notifications were not delivered to all 10,000 customers identified in the initial segmentation. Instead, the notifications were triggered by the customer’s recent activity on the Affiliate’s platform, meaning only 7,000 customers received the in-product advertising materials during the designated term year. The Affiliate reasoned that the remaining 3,000 customers were unlikely to interact with the content based on historical engagement data and thus excluded them from receiving the notifications. ACSI reported this campaign to Amazon as fully compliant, citing the total outreach numbers (10,000 customers) and the innovative delivery methods as evidence of meeting the contract’s obligations. 

Upon internal audit, Amazon’s compliance team flagged the campaign due to concerns about the mixed-brand emails and the incomplete delivery of in-product advertising. The ambiguity in the contract’s wording about delivery methods and the lack of clarity regarding how the minimum quantities applied to each delivery channel created significant debate over whether the campaign constituted compliance.

clauses.evidence_8: Except as specifically provided in the Distribution Agreement, Conformis shall be prohibited from developing or assisting another in developing, or causing another to develop, Patient-Specific Instrumentation for Off-The-Shelf Knee Implants for any Third Party in the field of orthopedics until January 1, 2032 (or earlier, to the extent set forth in Section 2.3.3.4 or Section 2.3.5 of the Distribution Agreement), with the exception that Conformis (including any entity involved in a Change of Control of Conformis, any such entity an "Acquirer"), may develop Patient-Specific Instrumentation for any Off-The- Shelf Implants of Conformis, an Acquirer or any of their Affiliates.

scenarios.scenario_text: Conformis enters into a partnership with Orthotech, a company specializing in Off-The-Shelf Knee Implants. Orthotech proposes a collaboration to develop Patient-Specific Instrumentation for a new line of implants targeting the adult sports medicine market, specifically high-performance athletes. Conformis reviews the governing clause and identifies that the prohibition against developing instrumentation for 'any Third Party in the field of orthopedics' includes exceptions for 'Off-The-Shelf Implants of Conformis, an Acquirer, or any of their Affiliates.' To align with this exception, Orthotech acquires 10% of Conformis' shares through a temporary equity transaction, becoming an Affiliate. After formalizing the partnership, Conformis develops the requested instrumentation, ensuring it is exclusively designed to be compatible with Orthotech's implants. However, during the development phase, Conformis allows Orthotech to subcontract a portion of the design testing to a third-party research lab, BioMedix Innovations, which specializes in orthopedic testing for multiple manufacturers. BioMedix uses the instrumentation prototype on implants from competing companies as part of its testing scenarios. Despite being aware of this practice, Conformis includes BioMedix's test results in its final deliverables to Orthotech. Conformis defends this decision, arguing that the subcontracting arrangement was under Orthotech's direct oversight and did not involve Conformis directly engaging with third parties in the orthopedic field. Meanwhile, internal communications reveal that Conformis executives acknowledged the ambiguity in the governing clause regarding 'causing another to develop' instrumentation for third parties. They decided not to take action to clarify the matter, citing potential delays to the partnership's timeline. Ultimately, Orthotech uses the instrumentation successfully, but competing manufacturers inadvertently benefit from BioMedix's testing data, creating grounds for questioning Conformis' compliance with its obligations.

scenarios.scenario_text: MSCI and MS are engaged in a reciprocal licensing agreement allowing each party to sublicense or create derivative works of the other’s licensed materials, provided that such actions are 'subject to any existing third-party contractual obligations.' MSCI develops a data visualization module derived from MS's licensed materials and sublicenses it to BetaCorp, a major industry player. BetaCorp had an outstanding exclusivity agreement with MS, but this agreement pertained only to 'standalone data analytics platforms directly distributed by MS.' MSCI argues that the sublicensed module is a derivative work and is therefore exempt from the exclusivity agreement. To expedite the deal, MSCI executed the sublicensing arrangement through an informal email exchange, bypassing a formal review by their legal team. However, the module heavily integrates MS’s core algorithms, which BetaCorp uses as part of its exclusive analytics platform. When MS discovers the deal, they claim MSCI's sublicense violates the exclusivity clause with BetaCorp and constitutes a breach of the licensing agreement. MSCI defends its actions by asserting that the exclusivity clause does not apply to derivative works sublicensed by MSCI, as the agreement only restricts MS’s direct distribution of analytics platforms. Additionally, MSCI claims no formal notification of BetaCorp’s exclusivity terms with MS was provided before execution, leaving them unaware of any potential conflict.

scenarios.scenario_text: Green Cross and MacroGenics are collaborating on the commercial development of MGAH22, governed by a detailed licensing and intellectual property agreement. During the Term, Green Cross grants MacroGenics a worldwide, royalty-free license under its patents and know-how 'to the extent needed' to develop and sell products. MacroGenics is also obligated to share updates on patent prosecution activities using outside counsel acceptable to Green Cross. A dispute arises when MacroGenics initiates legal proceedings against an infringing third party outside the Territory without providing Green Cross with a full opportunity to comment on the action, as required under the agreement. MacroGenics claims that it issued a notice via its internal project management platform, tagging Green Cross representatives in a comment thread outlining the intended legal action. However, the comment thread was archived after 24 hours due to MacroGenics' compliance team's automated system, leaving Green Cross unable to access the discussion or provide meaningful input. MacroGenics subsequently moved forward with the lawsuit, citing urgency to prevent further damage to the jointly owned patents. Green Cross challenges this decision, arguing that MacroGenics did not adequately 'permit Green Cross to participate' in the decision-making process as required under the governing clauses. MacroGenics defends its actions by asserting that its compliance with the 'to the extent needed' clause was sufficient, as the lawsuit was necessary to abate the infringement and protect the intellectual property.

RP's lead engineer, who is also the 'undersigned Receiving Party,' decides to expedite the evaluation process by involving an external consultant, Dr. Emily Carter, a renowned expert in algorithm optimization. Dr. Carter is not an employee of RP but has a long-standing professional relationship with the company and has signed a general non-disclosure agreement with RP in the past. The lead engineer emails Dr. Carter a detailed summary of the algorithm, explicitly marking it as 'Confidential' and requesting her feedback on its potential integration into RP's systems. Dr. Carter reviews the algorithm and provides valuable feedback, which RP incorporates into its evaluation. scenarios.scenario_text: In the final weeks of the Wind Down Period, DIALOG prepares to fulfill its obligations under a long-term supply contract with Customer Alpha. A senior operations director instructs a subcontractor, SubCo, via a verbal agreement to produce additional Licensed Products for Customer Alpha. This directive is issued following an internal meeting where the team discusses the urgency of meeting delivery deadlines and avoiding supply disruptions for Alpha, a key customer. The operations director argues that the verbal authorization is consistent with the agreement's language allowing subcontractor involvement during the Wind Down Period, as long as royalties are paid. To bolster this claim, DIALOG’s finance team ensures that all royalties owed to ENERGOUS are paid promptly, and a compliance officer emails ENERGOUS a summary of royalties paid. However, no formal written notice of subcontractor authorization is submitted to ENERGOUS, as required by Section 2.1. ENERGOUS later challenges this action, asserting that the lack of formal written notice invalidates the subcontractor's authorization, rendering the manufacturing activity unauthorized. DIALOG counters that verbal authorization and subsequent payment of royalties fulfill the spirit of the agreement and ensure customer satisfaction, a priority under the Continuing Obligation clause. The ambiguity surrounding the term 'including' in Section 2.1 leads DIALOG to interpret its obligations more broadly, believing informal authorization is permissible.

scenarios.scenario_text: Company A and Company B enter into a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) that defines 'Confidential Information' under clause 2.1 as including 'information relating to the existence of this Agreement.' Clause 2.2 provides an exception, stating that 'Confidential Information shall not include information developed or created by one Party independently of the other, without any part thereof having been developed or created with assistance or information received from the other Party.' Six months into the agreement, Company A launches a marketing campaign with the tagline: 'Our partnerships are built on trust and confidentiality.' The campaign is developed entirely in-house, and Company A’s legal team confirms that no input or information from Company B was used. However, during the campaign’s development, a senior marketing executive at Company A, who was aware of the NDA, privately consulted a former colleague (now a freelance branding consultant) for feedback on the tagline. The consultant was not informed of the NDA or the specific context of the campaign but provided general advice on how to make the tagline more impactful. The final version of the tagline was slightly modified based on this feedback. The campaign is launched, and an employee from Company B notices the tagline, interpreting it as a veiled reference to the NDA. Company B accuses Company A of breaching the NDA by disclosing the existence of the agreement. Company A argues that the campaign falls under the exception in clause 2.2, as it was developed independently without direct input from Company B, and the consultant’s feedback was unrelated to the NDA.

scenarios.scenario_text: The Distributor operates under an agreement with the Company that includes two key temporal obligations. First, the Distributor has the option to renew the agreement by providing prior written notice within ninety (90) days of the end of the initial period. Second, in the event of termination or expiration (for reasons other than breach by the Distributor), the Company is obligated to process orders accepted prior to the effective date of termination or within ninety (90) days thereafter. The initial agreement ends on July 31, 2023. On May 1, 2023, the Distributor sends an email to the Company formally indicating its intent to renew the agreement for an additional three-year period. On May 5, 2023, the Distributor submits a bulk purchase order to the Company for immediate processing, citing an urgent need to stock inventory for upcoming sales. This order is accepted by the Company on May 10, 2023. However, on June 1, 2023, the Distributor sends a revised email stating that it 'conditionally renews' the agreement, contingent upon favorable market conditions and supply chain stability. The Company interprets this as a conditional renewal rather than a definitive one. As a result, the Company begins preparations to wind down operations for the agreement's expiration on July 31, 2023, while continuing to process the May 5 bulk order to meet its obligations under the termination clause. On July 28, 2023, the Distributor submits a final declaration stating that it declines to renew the agreement, citing unfavorable market trends. The Distributor then argues that the Company remains obligated to process the May 5 bulk order under the termination clause, as the final decision to not renew does not retroactively alter the acceptance of the order. The Company disputes this argument, claiming the Distributor's conditional renewal email created ambiguity about the timing and validity of the renewal, thereby voiding the Distributor's ability to invoke both the renewal option and the termination clause for the same order.

scenarios.scenario_text: Erchonia enters into a distribution agreement with MedSupply Inc. ('Distributor'), granting it the right to promote, distribute, and sell certain medical devices ('Products') to licensed healthcare professionals in the United States, subject to additional qualifications in Exhibit B. The agreement also prohibits the export of Products outside the U.S. without Erchonia’s prior written consent. Exhibit B defines 'licensed healthcare professionals' as entities or individuals holding valid medical licenses, such as hospitals, clinics, or doctors, and stipulates that customers must maintain active certifications to operate the Products. MedSupply receives an order from MedSphere, a U.S.-registered telemedicine company that provides remote diagnostic services to international clinics. MedSphere’s chief medical officer, a licensed physician, signs the purchase agreement, and the Products are delivered to MedSphere’s U.S. warehouse. MedSupply’s sales team interprets MedSphere’s registration as a U.S.-based entity and the presence of a licensed medical professional as sufficient to meet the Exhibit B requirements. However, the Products are later disclosed to have been shipped to MedSphere’s international client, GlobalCare Clinics, for use in its facilities abroad. MedSupply does not inform Erchonia of the transaction, reasoning that the initial delivery occurred domestically and that MedSphere, as the primary purchaser, met the definition of a licensed healthcare professional. MedSupply’s compliance team later argues that the transaction adhered to the agreement terms since there was no direct export by MedSupply, and they had no control over MedSphere’s subsequent distribution actions.

scenarios.scenario_text: Maimon, a former consultant for the Company, had signed a non-solicitation agreement prohibiting them from suggesting to, inducing, or persuading any customer, client, vendor, supplier, employee, consultant, or agent of the Company to terminate or diminish their relationship with the Company during the term of the agreement and for two years thereafter. Seven months after the agreement's termination, Zenith Solutions approached Maimon, seeking recommendations for a highly specialized role. Maimon, who had previously worked closely with Sarah, a high-performing employee of the Company, believed she would be an excellent fit. Rather than reaching out directly to Sarah or advertising publicly on social media, Maimon contacted Sarah’s colleague, Tom, still employed at the Company, and stated, 'If Sarah is interested in exploring opportunities for growth, Zenith Solutions is hiring for a role that matches her skill set perfectly.' Tom, acting in good faith, informed Sarah about the opportunity, emphasizing that Maimon had spoken highly of her abilities. Sarah, intrigued, applied for and ultimately accepted the position at Zenith Solutions, leaving the Company shortly thereafter. The Company accused Maimon of violating the non-solicitation agreement, arguing that Maimon’s communication with Tom constituted an indirect attempt to induce Sarah to terminate her relationship with the Company. Maimon countered that their statement to Tom was merely an informational remark, not a solicitation, and that they never directly contacted Sarah or explicitly recommended that she leave the Company.

scenarios.scenario_text: Company A and Company B enter into a confidentiality agreement governed by the provided clauses. During negotiations, Company A shares a detailed presentation about its upcoming product launch with Company B via an email attachment. The email includes a brief note from Company A's representative stating, 'Please review this and let us know your thoughts. This is for internal use only.' The presentation itself is not marked with a 'Confidential' watermark, nor is the email sent through a secure, access-controlled platform. However, the email subject line reads 'Confidential: Product Launch Details,' and the attachment file name includes the word 'Confidential.' Company B later forwards the email, including the attachment, to an external consultant for feedback, believing that the lack of a watermark or secure sharing method indicated that the confidentiality designation was informal and not binding. When confronted, Company B argues that the email's subject line and file name were insufficient to meet the agreement's definition of 'Confidential Information,' which requires the information to be 'recorded, preserved, or disclosed' in a manner that clearly designates it as confidential. Company A counters that the subject line and file name, combined with the context of the email, were sufficient to meet the agreement's requirements, creating a dispute over the interpretive ambiguity of the term 'including but not limited to' in the governing clauses.

scenarios.scenario_text: Developer, a software company, has been in a long-term agreement with DSS that governs its intellectual property rights and operational autonomy. Facing financial strain, Developer decides to undergo a corporate restructuring. Instead of spinning off a new subsidiary as initially planned, Developer engages in a joint venture (JV) agreement with InnovateTech, a competitor in the software space. Under the JV, Developer transfers 55% of its software design team, patents related to its flagship product, and the associated operational assets to the new entity, InnovateDev LLC. Additionally, the JV agreement grants InnovateTech a 51% controlling interest in InnovateDev. Developer retains its headquarters, 45% of its design team, and the core intellectual property unrelated to the flagship product. Importantly, Developer interprets the term 'substantially all' in the DSS agreement as not applying to this transaction because the remaining assets and team are critical to its ongoing operations. Developer reasons that the retention of its headquarters and core IP ensures it has not transferred 'substantially all' of its assets. As such, Developer does not seek prior written approval from DSS, believing the transaction to be compliant with the agreement. In emails documenting the JV, Developer’s legal team internally discusses the ambiguity of 'substantially all,' concluding that the transaction does not meet the threshold for prohibition. Months after the JV is finalized, a competitor alleges that Developer’s transfer of a majority of its team and flagship product assets triggered the termination clause in the DSS agreement, arguing that the JV effectively constitutes the sale or transfer of 'substantially all' of Developer’s assets.

scenarios.scenario_text: CompuCom and Seller entered into an agreement involving the exchange of confidential information. Facing a critical cash flow crisis, Seller sought to secure a short-term loan from a private equity firm, Apex Capital. As part of the loan application, Seller disclosed historical financial information about the Business, including revenue trends, customer segmentation data, and pricing models. To expedite the process, Seller provided the information during a preliminary meeting without requiring Apex Capital to sign a formal non-disclosure agreement (NDA). Instead, Seller included a confidentiality clause in the footer of the presentation slides, which stated: 'By accessing this presentation, you agree to maintain the confidentiality of the information contained herein.' Apex Capital representatives verbally acknowledged the confidentiality clause during the meeting but did not sign any document explicitly agreeing to it. Seller justified its actions by citing Clause #3, which permits the disclosure of historical financial information, 'including financial information relating to the Business,' provided that third parties 'agree to preserve the confidentiality of such information.' Seller argued that the verbal acknowledgment and the confidentiality clause in the presentation slides satisfied the clause's requirements. However, CompuCom executives raised concerns, arguing that the lack of a formal NDA or written agreement created a significant risk of non-compliance and potential misuse of the disclosed information. They further contended that the clause's intent required a more explicit and enforceable agreement to ensure confidentiality, which was absent in this case.

scenarios.scenario_text: Company A and Company B are parties to a service contract that automatically renews for monthly terms unless either party provides written notice of termination at least 30 days before the current term's expiration. On January 1st, Company A, intending to terminate the agreement, sent a physical letter via standard postal mail to Company B, addressed to the company's corporate headquarters. The letter contained the following text: 'We are providing written notice of termination, effective at the end of the current term.' However, due to an internal delay at the postal service, the letter did not arrive at Company B's headquarters until January 6th. Upon receipt, Company B's legal team reviewed the notice and claimed that the agreement had automatically renewed because the notice was not received at least 30 days before the term's expiration as required under the contract. Company A argued that the contract specified 'written notice' but did not mandate specific delivery methods or confirm receipt dates, and that the use of standard postal mail was a commonly accepted practice for similar notices. Believing they had fulfilled their obligations, Company A ceased payments after January 31st, asserting the contract had been validly terminated.

clauses.evidence_3: The Company will compensate Consultant at the rate of $400 per hour (19 hours cap monthly; anything over these hrs must be preapproved by management), payable in accordance with the Company's standard payroll schedule, and subject to withholding as legally required.

scenarios.scenario_text: The Consultant submits an invoice for 22 hours of work in one month, explicitly noting that the additional 3 hours beyond the 19-hour cap were preapproved by the approving manager via an email exchange. However, upon review, the Company notices that the email only contains a vague statement from the manager saying, 'We’ll discuss the extra hours later,' without explicit approval. The Company processes payment for 19 hours at the agreed rate of $400/hour, with taxes properly withheld, and issues payment according to its standard payroll schedule. For the additional 3 hours, the Company decides to withhold payment entirely, asserting that the lack of explicit written preapproval violates the contract terms. To justify this decision, the Company relies on an internal policy requiring clear written authorization for any preapproval. After the Consultant protests, the Company offers to retroactively validate the hours if the Consultant can provide further clarification or supporting evidence from the manager. However, the approving manager is currently on extended leave, and no further documentation is immediately available. Weeks later, the issue escalates when the Consultant contacts legal counsel, arguing that the Company’s decision to withhold payment for the 3 hours is non-compliant with the contract because the ambiguous 'We’ll discuss later' email constitutes sufficient preapproval under the circumstances. The Company maintains its stance, claiming that its internal policy provides a reasonable interpretation of the contract. This creates a dispute centered on whether the vague email can be considered valid preapproval and whether the Company’s internal policy can override the contract’s explicit terms.

scenarios.scenario_text: Nantz Communications entered into a contract with The Company on January 1, 2023, requiring The Company to procure and maintain advertising insurance, product liability insurance, and Directors and Officers (D&O) insurance. The clause stipulated that The Company must submit fully paid policies or certificates within 30 days of the contract start date, naming Nantz Communications and Nantz as insured parties, and requiring 20 days' prior notice for termination or material modification. On January 29, 2023, The Company emailed scanned copies of the certificates to Nantz Communications, confirming the coverage limits as $5,000,000 for advertising and product liability insurance and $25,000,000 for D&O insurance. However, the email noted that the physical documents would be sent via regular mail, which would arrive approximately 5–7 business days later due to logistical delays. The email also included a summary of the D&O policy terms, stating that the insurer reserved the right to impose additional underwriting conditions in the event of a claim exceeding $10,000,000. This conditional language was not explicitly prohibited in the contract but raised concerns about whether the policy met the 'fully paid' requirement. Nantz Communications received the physical certificates on February 6, 2023, after the 30-day deadline. On February 9, 2023, Nantz flagged the submission as non-compliant, citing late receipt of physical documents and ambiguity surrounding the conditional underwriting terms. The Company's CEO defended the submission, arguing that the email on January 29, 2023, satisfied the delivery obligation since it provided all necessary information about the policies to Nantz Communications before the deadline. Additionally, the CEO asserted that the underwriting conditions were standard industry practice and did not affect the policy’s compliance with coverage limits.

clauses.evidence_5: Upon any expiration or termination of this Agreement, Emdeon shall have a reasonable period of time to remove the Content from the Software

scenarios.scenario_text: Emdeon entered into a licensing agreement with a software vendor, which included a clause stating that 'upon any expiration or termination of this Agreement, Emdeon shall have a reasonable period of time to remove the Content from the Software.' On March 1, 2023, the agreement was terminated with mutual consent. Emdeon’s compliance team notified their IT department to begin the removal process, but due to a concurrent migration of their internal systems, the IT department recommended a phased approach. On March 10, Emdeon sent a formal letter to the vendor stating, 'Removal of the Content is underway and will be completed in phases to minimize risk. We project final removal by July 15, 2023.' They also deactivated external access to the Content by March 15 to mitigate liability. However, the phased approach meant that Content remained fully accessible to Emdeon’s internal teams for operational purposes until July 15, 2023. The vendor, unaware of the phased timeline, assumed final removal would occur within 30 days of termination and expressed no objections at the time. When the vendor later discovered the internal access, they argued that Emdeon had exceeded a 'reasonable period of time.' Emdeon defended their timeline by pointing to the complexity of their internal migration and the need to ensure operational continuity. They also claimed that 'reasonable period' was undefined in the agreement, and their phased approach was a good-faith effort to comply.

scenarios.scenario_text: Customer, a technology services company, decides to assign its rights under the Agreement to a newly formed subsidiary, Customer Sub LLC, as part of a corporate restructuring. While Customer Sub LLC is legally classified as an 'Affiliate' of Customer, the assignment is structured in a way that involves a partial sale of Customer's assets to Customer Sub LLC. Specifically, Customer transfers 40% of its operational assets—primarily intellectual property and software licenses—while retaining the remaining 60% of its business operations. Customer argues that this transfer constitutes 'substantially all' of its assets under the assignment clause (Obligation Using 'substantial' #1), believing it satisfies the condition for assignment without Changepoint's consent. However, Customer does not notify Changepoint of the transaction. Following the transfer, Customer Sub LLC uses the rights under the Agreement to negotiate with a third party for strategic software integrations. Changepoint’s legal team later reviews the situation and disputes the assignment, claiming that transferring only 40% of Customer's assets does not meet the threshold of 'substantially all,' thereby violating the clause and rendering the assignment null and void.

scenarios.scenario_text: Party A and Party B enter into an agreement containing the multi-conditional non-solicitation clause outlined above. During the six-month non-solicitation period, Party A reaches out to Party B requesting a list of employees who might be available for collaboration on a future project. Party B provides a list of names and functions of its employees, explicitly stating that the list is for informational purposes only and not an invitation to solicit employment. However, Party A, instead of posting a general job advertisement as in the compliant scenario, decides to send a targeted email campaign to a curated list of professionals in the industry, including employees from Party B’s list. The email highlights a new role at Party A that matches the skill set of one of Party B’s employees. Party A does not directly address the email to Party B’s employees, nor does it mention Party B or its list explicitly. However, the email is sent to the personal email addresses of Party B’s employees, which Party A obtained from publicly available sources. One of Party B’s employees, who received the email, applies for the position and is subsequently hired by Party A. Party B raises concerns, claiming that Party A’s actions violate the non-solicitation clause, as the targeted email campaign indirectly solicited its employees. Party A argues that it adhered strictly to the clause, as the email campaign was a general industry outreach and the hiring resulted from the employee’s voluntary application.

scenarios.scenario_text: RevMed decides to explore licensing opportunities for a SHP1-SHP2 Dual Inhibitor with a Third Party. Per the agreement, RevMed is required to notify Sanofi in writing about its licensing decision and provide a detailed data summary before commencing negotiations. To streamline communications, RevMed opts to notify Sanofi by sending a formal email to Sanofi's designated legal contact. However, instead of directly attaching the required detailed data summary, RevMed includes a hyperlink to a secure online portal containing the data. The portal requires Sanofi staff to create individual login credentials and complete a two-factor authentication process to access the files. RevMed’s email emphasizes that this method ensures enhanced security and compliance with internal data protection policies. Due to technical difficulties and delays in credential setup, Sanofi’s internal team is unable to access the data immediately and misinterprets the incomplete access as a lack of proper notification under the agreement. This results in Sanofi missing its stipulated timeframe for issuing a 'Notice of Interest,' causing it to lose its exclusive negotiation rights. Sanofi claims RevMed failed to provide 'reasonable efforts' by using a method of delivery that created unnecessary barriers to accessing essential information, while RevMed argues that the notification was timely and compliant with its own internal security standards.

scenarios.scenario_text: HSWI and World Book entered into an agreement granting HSWI the right to renew under materially the same terms or purchase the Translated Content outright after a three-year period, provided rights permit and the parties mutually agree to terms. Additionally, HSWI received an eighteen-month right of first refusal for paid-subscription Chinese language websites using the Content. Approaching the end of the three-year term, HSWI sent a formal notice to World Book expressing its intent to renew the Agreement under 'substantially identical terms as previously agreed.' However, during the preceding year, HSWI had entered into negotiations with a third-party translation vendor to create derivative works of World Book’s Translated Content. While no agreement was finalized, the draft terms explicitly included provisions to use overlapping intellectual property rights. HSWI justified these negotiations by claiming they were merely exploring alternative options in parallel to their renewal discussions with World Book. Notably, HSWI’s renewal notice omitted any direct acknowledgment of the 'to the extent rights permit' condition, asserting instead that their continued use of the Translated Content under renewal was implicitly permitted under the original agreement. When World Book’s legal team reviewed the situation, they flagged the potential overlap in intellectual property rights and questioned whether HSWI’s negotiations with the third party undermined the mutual agreement requirement. HSWI defended its position by arguing that its renewal notice was valid as no specific format or conditions for renewal were explicitly outlined in the contract, and the exploratory negotiations with the third party had no legal bearing on the existing agreement. The ambiguity of the term 'to the extent rights permit,' coupled with the omission of explicit references in the renewal notice, created a plausible defense masking the underlying violation.

scenarios.scenario_text: ENERGOUS and DIALOG are parties to a licensing agreement that governs the use of Product IP and Deposit Materials. In early Q2, DIALOG identified an Epidemic Defect in a line of wireless charging units causing overheating and potential safety hazards. To address the issue urgently, DIALOG instructed its subcontractor, TechSolutions, to begin manufacturing corrections using Deposit Materials released from escrow. However, instead of issuing a formal written authorization, DIALOG relied on an internal project management system (PMS) task assignment feature, which included a brief instruction to 'use all necessary materials to resolve defect' tagged to TechSolutions' account. This assignment was marked as 'complete' once TechSolutions confirmed receipt, but no additional documentation was created, as DIALOG believed the PMS record was sufficient under Section 2.1. The corrections were completed, and DIALOG included this in its quarterly compliance report to ENERGOUS, attaching evidence of continued royalty payments and referencing the PMS log. ENERGOUS subsequently discovered that the PMS system did not explicitly reference 'Deposit Materials released from escrow,' nor did it include any formal acknowledgment of authorization per Section 2.1. ENERGOUS raised concerns that this informal mechanism created ambiguity about whether TechSolutions was properly authorized to use the Deposit Materials within the intended scope of fixing the defect. DIALOG argued that its use of the PMS system met the requirement to authorize subcontractor use under the 'including, but not limited to' clause, which it interpreted as allowing any reasonable method of authorization.

clauses.evidence_5: Pey Dirt has the right to terminate this Agreement immediately if Company's Endorsed Products are not being distributed in the Contract Territory to a significant number of stores by October 1, 1999.

scenarios.scenario_text: Pey Dirt, a distributor, was bound by a contract allowing them to terminate the agreement if the Company's Endorsed Products were not being distributed in the Contract Territory to a significant number of stores by October 1, 1999. On September 30, 1999, Pey Dirt conducted an internal audit and determined that the Endorsed Products were present in 51% of the stores deemed 'significant' in the Contract Territory. Concerned about the ambiguous threshold for 'significant,' Pey Dirt consulted its legal team. The lawyer advised that a majority presence (above 50%) could be interpreted as compliance, but Pey Dirt's executives opted to terminate the agreement anyway. At 10:00 AM on October 1, 1999, Pey Dirt sent a formal termination notice to the Company, citing failure to meet the distribution threshold. The letter was sent via certified mail with proper letterhead and signature, giving the appearance of procedural validity. However, Pey Dirt retroactively adjusted its internal audit findings to show only 49% distribution by reclassifying certain stores as 'non-significant,' ensuring the termination appeared justified. The Company argued that the audit manipulation violated the contract’s implied duty of good faith and accuracy. Pey Dirt defended its actions, claiming the contract did not define numerical thresholds for 'significant' or mandate specific audit procedures, and that their interpretation was reasonable given the lack of clarity.

scenarios.scenario_text: Company A and Company B are parties to a service agreement with an original term expiring on December 31, 2023. On November 1, 2023, Company A's legal team drafts a formal written notice of termination, explicitly stating the intention to terminate the agreement at the end of the original term. The document is signed by Company A's authorized representative and sent via certified mail to Company B's legal department. However, due to internal delays, the certified letter is not postmarked until November 2, 2023, and does not arrive at Company B's offices until November 6, 2023. Meanwhile, Company A also emails a scanned copy of the termination notice to Company B's designated representative on November 1, 2023, using the proper corporate email channel. The email subject line reads 'Termination of Agreement - Formal Notice,' and the attachment contains the signed notice in full. Company B acknowledges receipt of the email on the same day but later disputes the validity of the termination. Company B argues that the governing clause explicitly requires 'delivery' of the written notice at least sixty days before the term's expiration, which means that the physical certified letter had to arrive by November 1, 2023. They claim that the email copy does not satisfy the clause's requirement for 'written notice' since it is not equivalent to physical delivery by certified mail, which the parties had previously used for formal communications. Company A contends that the emailed copy fulfills the delivery requirement because it was sent and acknowledged on time, arguing that the certified mail was a redundant courtesy step.

scenarios.scenario_text: Recipient, a technology consulting firm, enters into a confidentiality agreement with Discloser, a software company, to evaluate a potential partnership. During the evaluation period, Recipient's employees attend brainstorming sessions where Discloser shares proprietary algorithms and business strategies. After the sessions, Recipient's employees create internal notes summarizing 'general ideas' and 'concepts' discussed, which are stored in a shared cloud-based document accessible to all employees of Recipient, regardless of whether they attended the sessions. Recipient argues that the term 'including' in the confidentiality agreement permits broader access to the notes, as it does not explicitly limit access to only those who attended the sessions. Subsequently, Recipient uses these notes to develop a proposal for a new software tool, which incorporates high-level concepts but avoids direct replication of Discloser's proprietary algorithms. Recipient ensures that all employees accessing the notes sign an internal confidentiality agreement requiring them to treat the information in accordance with the original confidentiality agreement. However, during a casual conversation at an industry networking event, one of Recipient's employees mentions that the brainstorming sessions were 'incredibly insightful' and helped them 'rethink their approach to algorithm design.' Discloser raises concerns, arguing that the broader access to the notes and the public comment constitute breaches of confidentiality. Recipient defends its actions, stating that the comment did not disclose any specific proprietary information and that the internal use of the information adhered strictly to the agreement's terms.

clauses.evidence_4: Upon termination of the Agreement, VerticalNet and Impresse shall jointly own all User Data.

scenarios.scenario_text: VerticalNet and Impresse entered into a partnership agreement, which stipulated in the Multi-Conditional Obligation clause that both parties would jointly own all User Data 'upon termination of the Agreement.' The partnership ended abruptly when Impresse's CEO, citing irreconcilable differences, sent a formal termination notice to VerticalNet late Friday evening. Concerned about data security over the weekend and anticipating potential system outages from Impresse's unstable servers, VerticalNet's IT team preemptively mirrored the User Data to a secure private cloud repository on Thursday morning—two days before receiving the termination notice. VerticalNet justified this early mirroring by pointing to an unrelated clause in the agreement that required 'reasonable steps to ensure data integrity during periods of operational uncertainty.' After receiving the termination notice, VerticalNet sent a formal email to Impresse stating, 'As agreed, the User Data has been secured to ensure operational continuity and is available for joint ownership. Please confirm receipt and advise on next steps.' However, VerticalNet’s early action created a timeline discrepancy: the data transfer occurred before the 'upon termination' condition was triggered. Impresse, already in financial distress, did not respond immediately to VerticalNet’s communication. Days later, VerticalNet publicly announced a new service update, stating, 'VerticalNet is committed to enhancing user experience with seamless access to data post-partnership.' This announcement included no reference to Impresse, causing external stakeholders to assume VerticalNet had unilaterally taken control of the User Data. Impresse’s bankruptcy trustees later objected, arguing that VerticalNet’s actions violated the joint ownership clause by executing the transfer before the contractual trigger event, undermining Impresse’s rights during the critical interim period.

scenarios.scenario_text: Company A and Company B entered into a licensing agreement with liability limitations structured around exclusions using the term 'including.' These exclusions are detailed in clauses evidence_8 and evidence_9, which exempt indirect, incidental, and consequential damages such as lost revenue or goodwill. During the partnership, a cybersecurity breach occurred due to a vulnerability in Company A's software. The breach exposed substantial customer data, triggering confidentiality obligations under Section 16. In response, Company A proposed a settlement to Company B, offering to cover direct remediation costs such as hiring forensic experts and providing customer notifications. However, Company A also offered a supplementary 'goodwill gesture' payment of $200,000 to address reputational harm and lost business, explicitly stating in an email that this payment was made 'outside the agreement's liability framework to preserve our strong partnership.' This email was sent by Company A's Regional Manager, who lacked the explicit authority for binding liability decisions as per Section 22 of the agreement, which mandates that only the CFO or General Counsel can authorize deviations from liability terms. Furthermore, Company A argued that the settlement aligned with the liability exclusions in evidence_8 and evidence_9, as the direct remediation costs were valid under Section 14's indemnity obligations, and the 'goodwill gesture' was discretionary rather than an acknowledgment of liability. However, Company B later discovered internal Company A communications revealing that the $200,000 payment had been calculated to partially offset anticipated lost business and reputational harm, which are expressly excluded as indirect damages under evidence_8 and evidence_9. This created a hidden violation, as Company A's offer indirectly circumvented the liability exclusions while presenting the payment as unrelated to contractual obligations.

clauses.evidence_6: NCB agrees that NPC may use NCB's name and its BIN, ICA and any other Visa and MasterCard identification numbers to the extent necessary or appropriate to perform the Merchant Processing Services.

scenarios.scenario_text: NCB operates as a payment processor and enters into an agreement with NPC to allow the use of its identification numbers, including BIN, ICA, Visa, and MasterCard IDs, under specific conditions outlined in Obligation Using 'to the extent' #2. NPC is tasked with performing Merchant Processing Services for a network of high-risk merchants, including cryptocurrency exchanges, which are subject to increased scrutiny by regulatory authorities. To streamline operations, NCB decides to grant NPC access to its identification numbers not through a shared folder, but by embedding the data into a proprietary API that NPC can query on demand. This API, while innovative, includes a feature that limits visibility of the identification numbers based on the perceived risk level of NPC’s merchants. Specifically, if a merchant is flagged in NCB’s internal risk database, the API will return null values, effectively withholding the identification numbers for those merchants. NCB justifies this approach by claiming it is ‘necessary and appropriate’ under the Agreement to mitigate risk exposure and ensure compliance with federal regulations for high-risk industries. NPC, unaware of this filtering mechanism, experiences unexplained processing failures when attempting to onboard certain merchants. These failures result in delayed onboarding, lost business opportunities, and complaints from merchants. When regulators investigate, NCB argues that it provided the identification numbers ‘to the extent necessary or appropriate’ but tailored access based on its internal risk assessment to protect against regulatory violations. However, NPC disputes this interpretation, arguing that the filtering mechanism impairs its ability to perform the Merchant Processing Services as intended, potentially breaching the Agreement.

scenarios.scenario_text: Company A and Company B entered into a licensing agreement containing liability limitations defined with the term 'without limitation.' During the agreement’s term, Company A experienced substantial losses due to a software defect in a product supplied by Company B, claiming lost business and profits as a result of the defect. The defect was linked to a critical security flaw that led to the exposure of sensitive customer data. Company B, upon receiving the claim, invoked the agreement's liability exclusions (evidence_8 and evidence_9) and capped its liability to $1,000,000, citing the intellectual property indemnification cap in the Enterprise License clause. However, instead of communicating its position formally, Company B addressed the issue in an internal email exchange, summarizing its liability stance and instructing its legal team to delay formal communication to 'allow time for technical mitigation.' Five days later, Company B sent a formal written notice to Company A, but the letter omitted any mention of the security flaw's broader implications, focusing solely on the monetary cap. Company B also issued a $500,000 refund (half of the $1,000,000 cap) on the grounds that the defect partially arose from third-party code incorporated into the product as of the Effective Date. This partial refund was justified as consistent with the agreement but was perceived by Company A as arbitrary, given the scale of damages incurred. Company A later discovered the internal email chain, which included a discussion about using 'ambiguity in the liability exclusions' to reduce exposure. This raised serious concerns about whether Company B acted in good faith and adhered to the notification and indemnification requirements outlined in the agreement. The dispute escalated when Company A accused Company B of exploiting interpretive ambiguity in the clauses to avoid full accountability for the defect’s consequences.
